subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 3-week-old boy born to a mother with untreated HIV infection is brought for evaluation. He is asymptomatic and his physical examination is normal, but maternal anti-HIV IgG antibodies are present in his serum, making serologic testing unreliable at this age.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate technique to determine whether the infant is infected?
explanation_correct: PCR amplifies a specific DNA segment using DNA primers, a heat-stable DNA polymerase, and deoxynucleotide triphosphates through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and elongation. In neonates, maternal anti-HIV antibodies cross the placenta and persist for months, so amplification-based detection of proviral DNA or viral RNA is used to establish infection; PCR is also used to diagnose herpes encephalitis from cerebrospinal fluid.

explanation_incorrect.B: Southern blot detects specific DNA fragments by size after restriction digestion and hybridization, but it is not an amplification method and lacks the sensitivity required for this diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Northern blot detects RNA species, typically to study mRNA levels and splicing, and is not used for neonatal HIV diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Western blot detects proteins with antibodies and is used to confirm HIV infection in adults, but it cannot distinguish maternal antibody from infection in a neonate.
explanation_incorrect.E: Karyotyping examines chromosome number and structure and is irrelevant to the diagnosis of HIV infection.

educationalObjective: PCR amplification is the preferred diagnostic test for neonatal HIV infection because transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies make serologic tests unreliable.
